text:
Der Asra 

Täglich ging die wunderschöne
Sultanstochter auf und nieder
Um die Abendzeit am Springbrunn,
Wo die weißen Wasser plätschern.

Täglich stand der junge Sklave
Um die Abendzeit am Springbrunn,
Wo die weißen Wasser plätschern;
Täglich ward er bleich und bleicher.

Eines Abends trat die Fürstin
Auf ihn zu mit raschen Worten:
Deinen Namen will ich wissen,
Deine Heimath, deine Sippschaft!

Und der Sklave sprach: ich heiße
Mohamet, ich bin aus Yemmen,
Und mein Stamm sind jene Asra,
Welche sterben wenn sie lieben.

space: A fountain with white, splashing water is the shared setting where the sultan’s daughter walks and a young enslaved man stands.
The sultan’s daughter moves back and forth beside the fountain, while the enslaved man initially remains stationary; their physical proximity contrasts with their unequal social positions.
Yemen is the homeland named by the enslaved man, Mohamet; it is an evoked place of origin, not the setting of the encounter.
time: The two figures appear at the fountain daily around evening, establishing a recurring twilight encounter.
Across these repeated evenings, the young enslaved man grows progressively paler.
One particular evening interrupts the daily pattern: the sultan’s daughter approaches the enslaved man and asks him to identify himself.
characters_or_voices: An unnamed, exceptionally beautiful daughter of a sultan walks beside the fountain each evening. Later called the princess, she approaches the enslaved man and demands his name, homeland, and kinship.
A young enslaved man stands beside the fountain each evening and becomes increasingly pale. When questioned, he identifies himself as Mohamet from Yemen and as a member of the Asra.
A third-person narrator describes the repeated encounters and the young man’s visible change without directly explaining either character’s inner thoughts.
The princess speaks in rapid, commanding direct speech; Mohamet answers with a concise declaration of identity that culminates in the claim that the Asra die when they love.
motifs: Daily recurrence: the same evening setting, fountain, and figures return until a single conversation breaks the pattern.
White splashing water and increasing human pallor: the fountain’s whiteness is visually echoed by the young man’s fading complexion.
Movement and stillness: the princess walks back and forth while the enslaved man stands; her eventual approach changes their spatial relationship.
Beauty and bodily decline: the princess’s exceptional beauty is juxtaposed with the young man’s increasing pallor.
Social inequality: a sultan’s daughter questions an enslaved man, placing their encounter within a hierarchy of rank and power.
Name, homeland, and kinship: Mohamet’s answer gives him a personal identity and an affiliation beyond his enslaved status.
Love linked to death: Mohamet describes the Asra as people who die when they love; no death actually occurs within the narrated action.
artistic_procedures: Four four-line stanzas organize the poem into repeated encounters, visible decline, questioning, and a final self-revelation.
Repetition of 'daily' and the nearly identical lines about evening, the fountain, and white splashing water creates a patterned, songlike recurrence.
The intensifying phrase 'pale and paler' compresses a gradual bodily transformation into a brief verbal progression.
Parallel descriptions place the princess and the enslaved man at the same fountain and hour while contrasting her walking with his standing.
The shift from habitual time to 'one evening' turns a recurring tableau into a singular dramatic encounter.
Direct speech replaces external narration in the final half of the poem, allowing the princess’s questions and Mohamet’s answer to carry the revelation.
The final statement about dying from love retrospectively suggests an explanation for Mohamet’s pallor without explicitly naming the object of his love.
The title, 'The Asra,' names the group whose significance is withheld until the closing lines.
atmosphere: A quiet, rhythmic evening atmosphere is sustained by repeated visits and the sound of splashing fountain water.
Visual beauty is shadowed by melancholy and growing unease as the young enslaved man becomes increasingly pale.
The princess’s rapid questions introduce urgency into the previously repetitive scene.
The closing association of love with death gives the encounter a restrained, ominous, and potentially tragic intensity.

elements_interpretation: The recurring evening fountain creates a shared space without erasing the social distance between the princess and the enslaved man. Her movement contrasts with his stillness, while the white water visually echoes his increasing pallor. Their conversation transforms him from an observed, unnamed figure into Mohamet, a person with a homeland and kinship. His final statement invites the interpretation that his bodily decline expresses love for the princess, although neither that love nor its object is explicitly declared. Death remains a stated association rather than a narrated event, leaving the ending suspended between self-revelation and possible tragic warning.

illustration.interpretation:
Beside a fountain in a richly ornamented courtyard, the princess leans toward a young man whose lowered head and slack arms contrast with her intent gaze. Her embroidered gown, gold jewelry, and translucent veil establish a visible distance from his torn, loosely wrapped clothing, even as they stand close together. The illustration concentrates on the evening when her approach breaks the pattern of repeated encounters: her forward posture suggests an urgent question, while his stillness gives the exchange a restrained, unequal tension. Arches, foliage, and a distant dome frame the scene without identifying it as Yemen, which belongs to Mohamet’s account of his origins rather than to the encounter’s visible setting.

The fountain’s bright spray rises between and behind the figures, echoing the young man’s pale complexion and setting its lively flow against his bodily withdrawal. Warm sunset light preserves the beauty of the evening, but his downcast face introduces melancholy into that beauty. The image cannot show his gradual fading across successive days; instead, it gathers that progression into a single moment of apparent depletion. His posture may suggest the burden of an unspoken love, though neither its object nor his inner thoughts become certain. Likewise, the closing association between love and death is rendered as vulnerability and foreboding, not as an actual death: he remains standing before the princess, poised at the threshold of the self-revelation that will give his silence a name and an affiliation.

animation.interpretation:
In a courtyard lit by lanterns beneath a fading evening sky, the princess advances toward Mohamet beside the fountain. Her flowing, richly ornamented dress contrasts with his loose, worn clothing, making their unequal positions visible even as the distance between them closes. He initially stands with his head bowed and his arms held behind him, while she supplies almost all the movement. As she reaches him, he raises his eyes; her open-handed gesture appears to ask for an answer, and his parted lips suggest the beginning of his reply. The animation thus concentrates on the moment when the poem’s recurring, largely silent encounter becomes a direct exchange.

The fountain’s bright white spray remains a persistent backdrop to this change, connecting the scene’s beauty with the motif of Mohamet’s pallor. His subdued bearing and pale face suggest vulnerability, although the animation does not clearly enact the gradual bodily decline described in the text. Nor does it depict Yemen, the Asra, or death: these remain beyond the visible encounter, leaving his emerging speech to carry the possibility of a larger identity and an ominous revelation. When the sequence returns to the princess’s distant approach, the moment of recognition gives way again to separation. This looping movement recalls the poem’s daily recurrence while repeatedly bringing the viewer to the threshold of the declaration that could explain Mohamet’s suffering.
